So it looks like they made certain connections/weights less malleable. Kind of interesting. So once it learns something, it becomes harder to unlearn something. Like a human becoming set in its ways. At the start a human is relatively completely malleable, but the more it learns the more it becomes resistant to change and new ideas. Try changing the politics of an old person, for example. In the same way, this AI learns the initial game, remembers, and then learns the next game, but it is not as good at the next game as it would have been if it started with that game in its completely malleable initial form. I can't help but wonder if they could make some sort of meta AI. So train 100 AIs to be near perfect on 100 games, and then feed the datasets of all 100 specialists into a general AI. I wonder if this would be any more effective than having one AI learn all 100 games with the memory rigidity algorithm being deployed here

The important part is (if Wired got this right) the ability to apply one task's knowledge to another. That's huge. A person can learn to throw a baseball, and then apply some of that knowledge to playing basketball. It's a whole other level of deep learning. And it may be the breakthrough we've been waiting for.

From my admittedly limited understanding of neural networks, what this sounds like to me is they slow down the learning rate on the few important weights for already learned tasks, and let the rest of the weights pick up the slack for new tasks. This doesn't necessarily mean that the knowledge transfers between games. It just means the same network can be used for multiple games. Which also means that it is functionally the same as training a bunch of smaller networks, just way less efficient. Perhaps there is a key point that I'm missing, but quite frankly this doesn't sound as impressive as the title makes it out to be.

Our study found an increased risk of hospital admission for heart failure in association with current use of several traditional NSAIDs (diclofenac, ibuprofen, indomethacin, ketorolac, naproxen, nimesulide, piroxicam, and possibly nabumetone) and two COX 2 inhibitors (etoricoxib and rofecoxib). We confirmed these findings after adjusting for multiple comparisons.
